# syntax


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

This module uses [spaCy](https://spacy.io) to detect long sentences,
stacked clauses, sentences with three or more punctuation-separated
sections, passives, and part-of-speech-dependent vocabulary. It also
checks noun clusters, nominalizations, actor placement, and phrases
whose meaning depends on their position in a sentence.
[`get_nlp`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#get_nlp)
downloads and loads the spaCy model.

``` python
from fastcore.test import *
```

## Getting the model

Slopometer uses spaCy’s 40MB `en_core_web_md` pipeline. The `md` and
`lg` English models share a vocabulary of 684,830 keys and the same
tagger and parser architecture. The `md` model maps that vocabulary to
20,000 shared vectors. The 560MB `lg` model keeps 342,918 vectors.

The rules use the parse and vocabulary membership, including `is_oov` in
the variation rule. They do not compare vector similarities. The `para`
notebook explains why the proposed similarity-based detectors failed. A
future rule that uses similarity would need its own model comparison.

Explosion publishes the model as a wheel on [GitHub
releases](https://github.com/explosion/spacy-models/releases), outside
PyPI. Slopometer downloads it separately rather than declaring a
direct-URL package dependency. `pip install slopometer` requires no
extra installation command.

[`model_path`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#model_path)
first checks for an installed model package. Otherwise, it downloads the
model to the user’s XDG cache directory on first use. The cached copy
serves projects across virtual environments and survives environment
syncs.

## Reading a parse

The rules use these spaCy token attributes:

- `pos_` is the part of speech, such as `NOUN`, `VERB`, `ADJ`, or `ADV`.
- `lemma_` is the dictionary form. It lets a rule match both “leverages”
  and “leveraged” with one entry.
- `dep_` and `head` describe the token’s grammatical relation to another
  token. For example, `nsubj` marks a subject and `dobj` an object.

The parser also finds sentence boundaries. Splitting on periods would
mishandle abbreviations such as “e.g.” and version strings such as
“v3.8.0”.

[spaCy 101](https://spacy.io/usage/spacy-101) introduces these concepts.
The labels relate to [Universal
Dependencies](https://universaldependencies.org/), although spaCy’s
English models use ClearNLP labels. Chapters 17-18 of [Speech and
Language Processing](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/) explain
statistical parsing. Parse errors can cause both missed findings and
false positives.

``` python
doc = get_nlp()('The gateway never kills an unresponsive kernel.')
L((t.text, t.pos_, t.lemma_, t.dep_, t.head.text) for t in doc)
```

    [('The', 'DET', 'the', 'det', 'gateway'), ('gateway', 'NOUN', 'gateway', 'nsubj', 'kills'), ('never', 'ADV', 'never', 'neg', 'kills'), ('kills', 'VERB', 'kill', 'ROOT', 'kills'), ('an', 'DET', 'an', 'det', 'kernel'), ('unresponsive', 'ADJ', 'unresponsive', 'amod', 'kernel'), ('kernel', 'NOUN', 'kernel', 'dobj', 'kills'), ('.', 'PUNCT', '.', 'punct', 'kills')]

## Sentence load

ASD-STE100 limits descriptive sentences to 25 words and procedural
sentences to 20.
[`find_sent_len`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_sent_len)
uses 25 words, excluding punctuation. It adds one weight point per extra
word when the sentence also contains at least two clauses. A
single-clause enumeration can exceed the cap without a finding.

[`_n_clauses`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#_n_clauses)
starts at one and counts these additions:

- Each subordinate clause labelled `advcl` or `ccomp`.
- Each coordinated verb with its own subject. “The kernel gains ports
  and clients see restarting” counts as two clauses. “Reads stdin,
  writes to the terminal, sees the same directory” does not add clauses.

Relative clauses such as “a small program that starts fast” do not
increase the count.
[`find_clauses`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_clauses)
flags counts of four or more, with one weight point per clause beyond
three.

[`find_tacked_semi`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_tacked_semi)
gives a semicolon a weight of 4 when both sides contain a subject
attached to a verb. It excludes semicolons inside parentheses, such as
citation separators. Lists of noun phrases or participles also pass.

Check the list and citation that the old rule misclassified, alongside a

``` python

    'The dimensions were settled long ago (SummEval; Fabbri et al., 2021).']
```

    [[4] semi_splice (tell 1, splices): ';']

A short sentence can still tack several clauses on with commas. “Inside
brackets, a space separates items, and a run of tokens with no spaces
between them is one item” has 19 words and two clauses. Neither
[`find_sent_len`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_sent_len)
nor
[`find_clauses`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_clauses)
flags it.

[`find_sections`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_sections)
flags sentences with three or more sections. The weight is one point for
each section beyond two. A section ends at a comma, semicolon, colon, em
or en dash, or spaced hyphen. A parenthesis adds a section, except
inside a list item. Punctuation inside parentheses does not end a
section.

List items stay in one section. A comma is a list separator when the
items after it have no subject of their own and include a coordinator
such as “and” or “or”. Three or more items without subjects also form a
list without a coordinator, as in “the target function, the interpreter,
the package versions”. A list at the start of a sentence can be the
sentence’s subject. spaCy then parses the last item as the subject, as
in “Printing, piping, and prompts therefore work exactly as if nothing
was in between”.
[`find_sections`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_sections)
keeps such a list together when its earlier items have no verbs. Text
inside parentheses does not count when deciding whether an item has a
subject or a verb. A comma after an opening phrase with no verb, such as
“Inside brackets,”, ends a section if the rest of the sentence has a
verb. A semicolon ends a section only where
[`find_tacked_semi`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_tacked_semi)
flags it.

[`find_tacked_and`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_tacked_and)
flags “, and” when the clause after it has its own subject. Its weight
of 3 matches
[`find_conseq`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/lexicon.html#find_conseq)’s
weight for “, so”.
[`find_sections`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_sections)
flags such a join only in a sentence with three or more sections.

The subject test relies on spaCy’s parse and has three known false
positives. The rule does not try to avoid them:

- A list that forms the sentence’s subject, such as “Printing, piping,
  and prompts therefore work exactly as if nothing was in between.”
  spaCy makes the last item the subject of the verb.
- A list of clauses, such as “how the code maps onto the world, why the
  code is the way it is, and how it can be sensibly extended.” Each item
  has its own subject.
- A relative clause after “and”, such as “and construct statements that
  were never in the text.” The test counts the relative clause’s
  subject.

## Passive voice

“The file is deleted” omits who deletes it.
[`find_passive`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_passive)
flags subjects labelled `nsubjpass`. Its findings weigh 0. Reports list
them, but they add nothing to the score.

The assertion below checks spaCy’s labels. A model change that renamed
`nsubjpass` would otherwise disable this rule without an error.

``` python
def find_passive(
    sent
):
```

*Passive constructions, listed without adding to the score*

``` python
ps = list(get_nlp()('The config file is read at startup. The socket was closed by the client.').sents)
test_eq([t.dep_ for t in ps[0]][:4], ['det', 'compound', 'nsubjpass', 'auxpass'])
passives = find_passive(ps[0]) + find_passive(ps[1])
test_eq([f.weight for f in passives], [0, 0])
passives
```

## Vocabulary judged by the parse

Some words are inappropriate only in particular uses. “The impact was
small” uses a noun. “This impacts performance” uses the verb where
“affects” would do. “The fix landed” leaves the reader to infer whether
it merged, committed, or released.

[`find_verb_banned`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_verb_banned)
checks part of speech and lemma. It excludes tokens after a hyphen, such
as the end of “aviation-shaped”.

[`find_intensifiers`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_intensifiers)
flags “simply”, “merely”, and “effortlessly” as adverbs. It excludes
“just” because the same part-of-speech tag covers both minimization (“it
just works”) and time (“just released”).

## Noun clusters and nominalizations

In “kernel connection state model update”, readers must work out which
noun modifies which.
[`find_noun_cluster`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_noun_cluster)
flags runs containing at least three common nouns and increases the
weight for each extra noun. Proper nouns do not count toward the
threshold. “New York City subway” passes.

A nominalization expresses an action as a noun: “make a decision”
instead of “decide”.
[`find_nominalization`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_nominalization)
checks for a light verb with a derived noun as its object. It suggests a
verb from a fixed mapping, such as “assess” for “perform an assessment”.

## Actor placement

Joseph Williams’s *Style: Toward Clarity and Grace* recommends making
the doer the subject and the action the verb. Tells 22 and 23 cover two
ways prose can obscure the doer:

- Artifact-as-agent credits a document or change with its author’s
  action: “this PR introduces”.
- Recipient-as-subject describes what the beneficiary receives: “the
  kernel gains fresh ports via the new process”.

[`find_artifact_agent`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_artifact_agent)
requires an authorship artifact as subject and a verb from its crediting
list. “The parser rejects malformed input” passes because the parser
performs that operation.

[`find_recipient_subject`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_recipient_subject)
flags “gain” and “receive” when they have a subject. It flags “get” only
with a “via” or “through” phrase.

A third way gives an act to something that cannot perform it. “The
positions decide the result’s shape” credits a value with the caller’s
choice. “A single position removes its axis” credits it with what the
function does.

[`find_inert_mind`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_inert_mind)
flags a common noun that is the subject of a verb from `_mind_verbs`,
acts that need a mind such as decide, own and prefer. These findings
belong to tell 22, because a person made that choice.
[`find_inert_act`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_inert_act)
flags the same subjects with a verb from `_act_verbs`, physical or
deliberate acts such as carry, stamp and remove, under tell 11. Its
findings weigh 2, against 3 for
[`find_inert_mind`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_inert_mind).
Nouns in `_people` and `_runners` pass with any verb: people and roles
such as user and author, and components that run such as parser, server
and function.

### find_inert_act

``` python
def find_inert_act(
    sent
):
```

*Subjects that cannot act, given a verb for a physical or deliberate
act*

The lists started from seed words and grew with `en_core_web_lg` vector
neighbours, reviewed by hand. The rules skip pronouns, proper nouns,
inline code and nouns capitalised mid-sentence, because they cannot
judge what these refer to. A capitalised noun mid-sentence is usually a
tool or API name, such as “Scrub” below. Nouns that act in one project
and not in another, such as rule and operator, stay off `_runners` and
give false positives. Quoted mentions give false positives too.
Components that run pass even with a verb of the mind, as “The scheduler
decides which task runs next” shows:

``` python
inert_sents = ["The positions decide the result's shape.", "A single position removes its axis.", "A space makes a train.", "Rows carry their source."]
actors = ["The parser rejects malformed input.", "The user decides which file to load.", "The scheduler decides which task runs next.",
    "It removes the axis.", "Each row has a key.", "After parsing, Scrub keeps the text runs."]
def inert(s): return find_inert_act(list(get_nlp()(s).sents)[0]) + find_inert_mind(list(get_nlp()(s).sents)[0])
for s in actors: test_eq(inert(s), [])
fs = [f for s in inert_sents for f in inert(s)]
test_eq([(f.tell, f.weight) for f in fs], [(22, 3), (11, 2), (11, 2), (11, 2)])
fs
```

## Sentence-anchored patterns

Position matters for some phrases. “This section describes” announces
content at the start of a sentence, but “the part this section
describes” has another purpose.
[`sent_rule`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#sent_rule)
can restrict a phrase list to sentence starts.

The phrase rules cover throat-clearing, today’s-world openers,
announce-then-deliver, not-X-but-Y, teasers, and appraisal preambles.
[`find_rhetorical`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/syntax.html#find_rhetorical)
separately flags sentences ending in a question mark.

The not-X-but-Y rule limits its matches to patterns such as “isn’t just
a”. It leaves contrasts such as “not thread-safe, but lockable” alone
because they can state useful constraints.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/slopometer/blob/main/slopometer/syntax.py#L351"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### sent_rule

``` python
def sent_rule(
    name, # Rule name, as in `core.rule`
    tell, # `write_docs` tell number
    weight, # Tier the findings carry
    pats, # Phrase list; each becomes a case-insensitive regex alternative
    anchored:bool=False, # Match only at the sentence start?
):
```

*Build and register a sentence rule that scans `pats` in the sentence
text*

``` python
checks = ["This section describes how the gateway manages the kernel lifecycle.",
    "So what does restart actually do?", "It isn't just a poller - it's the liveness authority.",
    "The distinction is worth being precise about.", "The core mechanism: watch."]
found = L(f for s in checks for sent in get_nlp()(s).sents
    for f in find_throat(sent)+find_rhetorical(sent)+find_notxbuty(sent)+find_appraisal(sent)+find_announce(sent))
test_eq(find_notxbuty(list(get_nlp()('The list is not just names, and callers must not assume order.').sents)[0]), [])
found
```

    [[3] throat_clearing (tell 13, throat-clearing): 'This section describes', [3] rhetorical (tell 18, rhetorical questions): 'So what does restart actually do?', [10] notxbuty (tell 16, not-X-but-Y): "isn't just a", [3] appraisal (tell 21, appraisal preamble): 'worth being precise', [3] announce (tell 15, announce-then-deliver): 'The core mechanism: ']
